preamble: The shift from the velar nasal [ŋ] to the alveolar nasal [n], often colloquially called 'G-dropping', is a common sociolinguistic phenomenon in English and other languages. It typically occurs in unstressed syllables where the place of articulation moves forward from the soft palate to the alveolar ridge.

examples.note: Unstressed morpheme-final -ing /ɪŋ/ is realized as [ɪn] or [ən] (spelled -in'); stereotyped in U-RP 'huntin', shootin' and fishin'' and common in casual registers across North American and British accents. Monosyllables such as sing and king are not affected.
Hakka velar codas tend to become dental after front vowels.
-en/-eng and -in/-ing merge in the Southwest, so 金 and 京 are homophones; Standard Mandarin jīng [tɕiŋ].
*ŋ merged with n in Hawaiian, alongside *t > k; cf. Māori tangata, Tahitian taʻata (*ŋ > ʔ)
